1.pericope_label: The Spirit speaks expressly: a departure from the faith in the latter times

schools.summary: Open on the adversative: the verse stands in deliberate contrast to the mystery of godliness just celebrated, and the contrast is the point. Locate the prophecy honestly — the Thessalonian parallel shows the substance had been preached before, and the adverb, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, means in express words rather than by hint or symbol. Do not soften the extent: the indefinite pronoun does not promise a small number. Then hold the line on the last clause. The seducing spirits are not a periphrasis for false teachers but evil powers, and the ambiguity of the genitive in doctrines of devils is real: if the previous clause already says taught by demons, this one most likely means taught about them.

Preach it as a prophecy about worship, not merely about morals. The apostle opens with a solemn preface precisely because the danger is one the church will not see coming: men are by nature inclined to think God is served by ceremonies and outward discipline, and Satan confirms the error. Note who is said to fall — the hearers, since the teachers are named separately in the next clause, and the graver point is that impostors never lack disciples. Then answer the objection that the description is too vague to identify anyone: it is not, because the marks are given. The controversy is not about flesh or fish or about which day of the week, but about men who assume dominion over conscience and forbid what God has permitted; and once the purity of worship is impaired, faith itself is ruined.

Fix the timing first: the latter times are not the closing years of the world but the whole span from the ascension to the judgment, so the prophecy has been running the entire time. Do not let apostasy be reduced to open denial. A man may hold every Christian truth and render it of none effect by other doctrines that counteract it, or deny one essential article while bringing in nothing formally heterodox. On the last clause note the reading of many manuscripts and the chief fathers, spirits of deceit, which is the more emphatic; and take the demons in the wide sense, whether fallen spirits or the spectres of the dead, since it is doctrine about these that Satan uses.

Set the two mysteries side by side: the previous chapter summed up the mystery of godliness, so this one sums up the mystery of iniquity. Draw the doctrinal inferences the verse will bear — that the Spirit must be God, since events depending on the tempers and lusts of men cannot otherwise be foreseen, and that the plainness of this word is exactly what distinguishes it from the heathen oracles, which were always doubtful. Then give the comfort that is in it. The word is some, not all: in the worst of times God will have a remnant according to the election of grace. Identify the doctrine of demons as the worship of saints and angels as a middle order of deities, which is paganism revived.

Begin with the image rather than the argument: those who hold the faith are fixed on a safe anchor, while those who fall from it can nowhere rest, and after much wandering are carried into the gulf of perdition. Name the sects the prophecy fits — Manichaeans, Encratites, Marcionites — and refuse the easy application to the Jews, since neither the latter times nor a departure from the faith can be said of them. Insist that the lie is deliberate: these men do not err through ignorance but act a part, knowing the truth. And use the verse where it does most work outside its own context, as proof that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives, speaks and foretells.

debates.question: Does 'some shall depart' promise that the apostasy will be limited?

sides.position: Some, not all: in the worst of times God will have a remnant according to the election of grace, and this is a comfort in the text
The word does not imply a small number; the parallel prophecy points to an apostasy of great extent, and by degrees the far greater part will fall

debates.question: Are the 'doctrines of devils' taught BY demons or ABOUT them?

sides.position: Taught and suggested by evil spirits; the seducing spirits must not be watered down into false teachers
Teaching concerning demons; since the previous clause already says by evil spirits, the apostle would not immediately repeat himself, so this names a prevalent doctrine about invisible middle powers
Either, or both — demons meaning fallen spirits, or dead men and spectres, or doctrines inspired by Satan concerning these

debates.question: Of whom is the falling away predicated?

sides.position: Of the hearers, since the teachers are named separately as impostor spirits in the next clause; the sting is that seducers never want disciples
Of professing Christians generally, whose apostasy is worked through a hypocritical ministry

outliers.note: Alone frames the whole prophecy as being about the corruption of worship rather than about heresy in doctrine, and alone answers the objection that Paul's description is too vague to identify anyone. His formulation is the sharpest in the chapter: the controversy is not about flesh or fish, or about a black or ashy colour, or about Friday or Wednesday, but about men who contrive a carnal worship and so contrive an idol instead of God.

Alone reads the verse for its doctrine of the Spirit rather than its prophecy of apostasy, citing it as proof that the Holy Ghost subsists, lives, speaks and foretells, with the divisions of the heretics in his own day as the fulfilment.

Alone builds on the adversative particle, reading the verse as a deliberate contrast with the mystery of redemption at the close of the previous chapter, and alone gathers the New Testament instances of the Spirit's direct intimation to the first generation as the class to which this revelation belongs.

themes: Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;

2.pericope_label: Through the hypocrisy of men that speak lies, branded in their own conscience

schools.summary: Correct the received construction before anything else. The phrase is not that demons speak lies in hypocrisy but that men fall away through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies: the word order would have to be inverted for the other sense, and that sense, once adopted, must be carried through the sentence until demons are the ones forbidding marriage. The consequence is the teaching point — every characteristic that follows belongs to the teachers, not the taught, so the apostasy comes about through a hardened ministry. Then render the last clause branded rather than seared: the image is the mark burnt into slaves and criminals, and the verb is rare enough to stand here and once in Strabo and nowhere else.

Take the participle as describing the agents of the apostasy, not its victims, and press the hypocrisy: these are men who deliver false doctrine under the colour of truth and make great pretensions to holiness, which is exactly what takes with common people and leads them aside. Name the doctrines — merit, purgatory, invocation of saints, fastings, pilgrimages — together with the legends of the saints and the wonders reported of their relics, and observe that the whole apparatus is worked under a show of godliness and the promotion of religion.

Keep the two halves together: the lies and the cauterised conscience describe one man. On the lies, work from documents rather than assertion — a king's letter petitioning for a canonisation on the strength of the blind receiving sight and the lame walking, and the plain rejoinder that a saint who works no miracles now never worked any. On the second clause, the mark is the point rather than the numbness: these men carry their hypocrisy as indelibly in conscience before God as branded criminals carried their crimes in the body before men, and the heathen supposed such marks legible in the world to come.

debates.question: Does 'seared with a hot iron' mean made insensible, or branded with a mark?

sides.position: Cauterised, and so dead to feeling: the burnt part becomes rigid and insensible, and such a conscience will practise fraud without wincing
Branded, and so marked: the image is the mark burnt into slaves and criminals, and these men carry the brand of Satan as Paul carried the marks of Christ

debates.question: What are the lies?

sides.position: The doctrines and legends of Rome — merit, purgatory, invocation of saints, the miracles of relics
The teaching that abstinence from meats and from marriage pleases God, resting on Oriental speculation about the evil nature of matter

outliers.note: Alone supplies private testimony as evidence, reporting that a gentleman of high authority told him that in France and Italy young men enter the Catholic ministry sincerely, learn in the course of their studies what the system rests on, and are by then committed past retreat — his argument that the lies are told knowingly rests on this as much as on the learning of the clergy.

Alone declines the Reformation application entirely, keeping the lies in the first century as ascetic teaching about meats and marriage, and alone identifies the root as speculation about the evil nature of all matter rather than as clerical fraud.

Alone closes with a pagan parallel, quoting Claudian's Rhadamanthus turning on Rufinus — why deny what is manifest, when the deep-burnt marks deform thy conscience and the crimes cannot hide themselves.

themes: Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron;

3.pericope_label: Forbidding to marry and to eat: every creature of God is good

schools.summary: Set the two prohibitions in their first-century home before applying them anywhere else: the Essenes, the Therapeutae and other oriental sects had already made abstinence from marriage meritorious, and the Colossian letter shows Paul condemning the same ascetic practice. Note the asymmetry and account for it — celibacy is dismissed in a sentence because it so plainly contradicts the order of creation, while abstinence from meats gets argument because it could be defended out of the Mosaic restrictions and so threatened to divide Gentile congregations from Jewish. Paul's answer lifts the question at once: all food comes from one Maker, and to call any of it unclean is an insult to the Creator. Then guard the sentence about every creature being good — it means good in its place and for the end intended, not good for every use to which men can put it.

Do not let the verse be spent on ancient sects. The Encratites, Montanists and Manichees spoke against marriage, but what the text describes is forbidding it in an authoritative way, which points at a priesthood that prohibits marriage to its own clergy under a pretence of purity while tolerating uncleanness. Carry the phrase about hypocrisy forward into every clause that follows: through the hypocrisy of those whose consciences are seared, and through the hypocrisy of those who forbid marriage — since it is precisely the appearance of great purity that draws the common people into the deception. On the food, keep it simple: every creature made for food is good, at all times, without distinction, and is set apart to that use by God's own word and by prayer.

Name the target plainly — priests, monks and nuns forbidden to marry, and men commanded to abstain from such and such meats at such and such times — and then ground the answer in the grant of Genesis, where God gave the herb and the moving thing for meat. That command is what sanctified the food; prayer is how a man sets it apart to its use for himself. Give the three ends of that prayer: that the food may answer its purpose, that it be used with gratitude and moderation, and that the strength drawn from it be spent in the duties providence has laid on us. Close hard: those who never thank God for their food are unworthy of the breath they breathe.

This is the passage where a fasting church must state its own rule carefully, and the distinction is exact. We abstain from wine and flesh not because we abhor them as abominations but because we look for a reward, having scorned things sensible so as to enjoy a spiritual feast. Everything the apostle condemns lies in the abhorrence, not in the abstinence. Therefore despise not those who eat, and do not blame those who take a little wine for the stomach's sake and their frequent infirmities; condemn no man as a sinner for eating, and abhor no flesh as strange food.

debates.question: Whom does the prohibition of marriage describe?

sides.position: The Essenes, Therapeutae and oriental sects of the apostle's own day, whose counsel of perfection later hardened into the dogma of the Gnostic schools
Not the ancient sects, who only spoke against marriage, but a clergy that forbids it authoritatively
Both: the sentiment was held by the Essenes and is now enforced by a vow of continency

debates.question: What sanctifies the food?

sides.position: The word of God in the grant of Genesis, which set food apart to that use, together with the prayer by which a man appropriates it
God's authority or permission, so that no command of man can make it unholy
Not any one grace before meat, which too often degenerates into heartless lip-service or is treated as a charm, but the habit of referring everything to the giver

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse on the temperance question of his own century, arguing that good means good in its place, that a poisonous liquid distilled from rye or Indian corn is no longer the creature God made, and that the passage must not be adduced to vindicate the use of intoxicating drinks.

The only voice here who fasts, and the only one who separates the practice from the error condemned, laying down that abstinence is not abhorrence and forbidding both the contempt of those who eat and the condemnation of those who do not.

Alone asks why celibacy is dismissed in one sentence while abstinence from meats is argued at length, and alone answers it: the celibate counsel refutes itself against the scheme of creation, whereas the food question could be supported from the Mosaic law and so had to be lifted to higher ground.
Alone hears a proverb behind the clause about nothing being refused, citing the heathen form from Lucian that the gifts which come from Jove are not to be despised.

themes: Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

6.pericope_label: A good minister nourished in the faith; refuse profane and old wives’ fables

schools.summary: The verb rendered put in remembrance means to place under, to suggest, and stands here alone in the New Testament — so the good minister is defined by what he keeps before people rather than by what he invents. Take the participle behind nourished up as a present, marking a continuous process: ever training thyself, with the education of a teacher never to be considered finished. The clause about attaining means followed closely, side by side, so the charge is to carry an early training out to its results. On the fables, restrain the adjective: profane does not mean blasphemous, only wanting the character of true religion, and the compound behind old wives' means the sort of tale told to children. The remedy is the gymnasium — not a metaphor for effort in general but for training directed at a contest.

Set out what is to be commanded and what taught: the rejection of profane and fabulous doctrine on the one hand, and on the other the exercise of true godliness with the promises that belong to it. Let the things in view be the substance of the letter so far — that the end of the commandment is love, that Christ came to save the chief of sinners, that prayer is to be made for all men — together with the prophecy just delivered. Identify the fables without narrowing them prematurely: they may be the traditions of the elders, or Gnostic speculation about God and angels and the creation, or the very doctrines of demons already condemned, and all are to be rejected with abhorrence in comparison with the words of faith.

Preach it as a warning that the danger is present, not future: show the church that even now there is occasion for this apostasy, since the forewarned are half armed. Then take the fables in both directions at once — the Talmudic writings on the one hand, and on the other the Golden Legend and the lives of the saints, which may be set column for column against them, with miracles more numerous and more stupendous than all the necessary ones wrought by Christ and his apostles. Close on the training image and make the comparison exact: the Greek athlete trained for a chaplet of leaves that withered, and this training is for a crown that does not fade.

Let the verb define the office. Those are good ministers of Jesus Christ who are diligent in their work, not those who study to advance new notions but those who put the brethren in remembrance of what they have already received — which is how Peter and Jude understood their own work, because we are apt to forget and slow to learn the things of God. Draw out two things the passage assumes: that ministers themselves must be growing, and that the way to grow is to teach, since while we teach others we teach ourselves. And mark the word brethren: those whom ministers teach are to be treated as brethren, for ministers are not lords of God's heritage.

debates.question: What are the profane and old wives' fables?

sides.position: The Rabbinic schools and their investigation of every book and almost every letter, in which the spirit of the writers was lost and legend grew so thickly that true and false could not be separated
The Talmud, and with equal propriety the legends of Rome — the Golden Legend and the lives of the saints
Any of three: Jewish tradition, Gnostic speculation about God and angels, or the doctrines of demons just condemned

outliers.note: Breaks frame twice in one verse: having found the verb for nourishing used by Plato of men nourished in the laws, and having called the words of the faith the right diet for babes in Christ, he adds without transition that the Bolshevists in Russia are feeding the children on atheism to get rid of God.

Alone turns the warning back on ministers themselves, observing that asceticism is a winning school for a teacher precisely because at a comparatively easy price it wins him a great and thoroughly unhealthy power over the souls of those who practise the austerities — and that a good minister must therefore teach a life which all can lead and not a select few.

Alone reads the clause about Timothy's training as a charge laid on the young generally: their friends' cherished hopes are a proper ground of appeal, and no young man should by neglect, indolence or folly disappoint the reasonable expectations formed of him.

Alone records the dissent of Schoettgen, who confined the whole prophecy to the Jews and denied any reference to a later church that might corrupt the doctrine, noting that Bishop Newton and others are of a different opinion.

themes: If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained.
But refuse profane and old wives’ fables, and exercise thyself rather unto godliness.

8.pericope_label: Bodily exercise profits little; godliness has promise of both lives

schools.summary: Decide first what the bodily exercise is, because the whole verse turns on it: the austerities of verse three, not athletics and not health. Then weigh the little. The phrase can mean for a little while or for little, and the answering clause — profitable for all things — argues for extent rather than duration. Do not overstate the condemnation: such training has in fact lifted individuals to a higher spiritual state, and the real harm is that the rigid ascetic steps off the platform on which ordinary men and women move, so that his thoughts cease to be their thoughts and his influence, always narrow, becomes harmful to everyday life. Set godliness against it as an operative piety whose reach is world-wide. On the last clause, distinguish the two senses in which God is Saviour of all: potentially of all, actually of the faithful.

Work through the possible senses of bodily exercise and reject them one by one — not the Olympic games, though the previous verse borrows their language; not riding or walking or any innocent diversion; not the labour of a trade; not even the mortifications of watching and fasting — and settle on mere formal external worship as opposed to spiritual worship, which is the contrast the verse actually draws. Then say what the labour and reproach were: not preaching, not inward exercise, not working with their own hands, but stripes and imprisonment, weariness and pain, watchings and fastings, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness.

Take bodily exercise at face value first — it does increase the health and strength of the body, and that is exactly the little profit granted — then set beside it the gymnastic exercises of the Greeks, esteemed and short-lived, referring only to this life and the applause of men. Godliness means everything the Christian religion promises or prescribes, the life of God in the soul of man. Guard the promise for this life against misuse: it does not mean exemption from natural evils, and the next verse is there precisely to prevent that inference, since it is because they exercise themselves to godliness that they have labour and reproach. On Saviour of all, hold the whole offer open — all have been purchased, all may believe, and those that perish perish through their own fault.

debates.question: What is the bodily exercise that profits little?

sides.position: Literal physical exercise, which does increase the health and strength of the body
The ascetic mortifications of verse three — abstinence and penance as a means of religion
The gymnastic exercises of the Greeks, of short duration and looking only to this life and the applause of men
Mere formal external worship, as opposed to the spiritual worship the verse sets against it

debates.question: In what sense is God the Saviour of all men?

sides.position: As preserver of all from famine and war and peril, and as provider of a salvation offered to all — but only believers are actually saved
He has provided and freely offered salvation for the whole race; what he intends for all he actually gives to those who believe, and those that perish perish through their own fault

The living God is also a loving God, Saviour of all if they would receive him — a saying aimed at Hebrew exclusivism, not a warrant for universalism, though the atonement's consequences may reach past sober speculation

debates.question: What does the faithful-saying formula point to?

sides.position: Backward, to the words just spoken about godliness — unlike its earlier occurrence in the letter, which points forward
To a watchword already current in the first congregations, drawn now from a hymn and now from a public prayer

outliers.note: Alone converts the promise for this life into a social claim, arguing that godliness prospers a man in business by making him sober and prudent, that every man privately believes he would be a Christian if he were ever certainly to be happy, and that true piety sends nobody to the alms-house, few of whose inmates give any evidence of religion.

Alone defends what he has spent three verses attacking, granting that ascetic training has in many cases led an individual to a higher spiritual state, is in a certain sense profitable, and received a guarded commendation from the lips of the Sinless One — so that Paul stops short of entire condemnation.

Alone reads the tenth verse as a deliberate correction of the eighth, stating that it was necessary to explain what had gone before, because the apostle did not mean that the followers of God enjoy worldly prosperity and exemption from natural evils.

themes: For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.
For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.

11.pericope_label: Let no man despise thy youth: be an example of the believers

schools.summary: Read the youth clause as a charge to give no occasion rather than as a licence to insist on deference — act so that nobody shall have grounds to despise you. Then take the six graces one at a time, because they are not interchangeable. The first covers conversation as much as public speech; the second is badly served by the old rendering and means manner of life or bearing; the third is absent from the older authorities altogether and should be handled as a textual question, not preached as a distinct grace; faith stands among graces, not doctrines; and the last word, used of a Nazirite, means sinlessness of life. Deny firmly that it enjoins celibacy: there is nothing in the word to support making virginity more honourable than the relation God appointed in Eden.

Distinguish the two verbs and apply them to the chapter just closed: command the rejection of the fables and the exercise of godliness, teach its profitableness and declare the promises annexed to it. On the youth, gather the evidence rather than asserting: Timothy may have been about three and twenty, though Saul was called a young man at thirty or more, and God has often honoured young men with great gifts for use in church and state — Samuel, David, Solomon, Daniel and his companions. The apostle's sense is that a man in office should not suffer himself to be treated with contempt, but exert his authority and magnify his office.

Reduce the first verse to a preaching programme — that true religion is profitable for both worlds, that vice destroys body and soul, that Christ tasted death for every man, and that he saves to the uttermost all who believe. On the youth, be concrete: gravity and decorum become the situation, and boyish playfulness ill becomes a minister of the gospel whatever his age. Press the example hard, since the flock follows the shepherd and men will excuse their own sins by saying that the minister does the same; if they went wrong through the watchman's fault, their blood will God require at his hand. Take faith here as fidelity, and on purity pass on the old advice to converse sparingly with women, and especially with young women.

Keep it short and practical: men's youth will not be despised if they keep from vanities and follies, and those who teach by doctrine must teach by life. The discourse must be edifying and the conversation holy, with the minister an example of love to God and to all good men, and of spiritual-mindedness. Say plainly what such duties exclude — they leave no leisure for worldly pleasures, trifling visits or idle conversation, and little enough for what is merely ornamental.

Make the two verbs a rule of pastoral judgement, because getting them the wrong way round is ridiculous in either direction. Wickedness is to be forbidden with authority, not reasoned about; parting with possessions, professing virginity, discoursing of faith are matters for teaching. Test it on a case: a man who wears an amulet knowing it wrong needs a command, and the man who does it ignorantly must be taught. Then resolve the difficulty the next clause raises — if a teacher is not to be despised, where is the room for meekness? Contempt offered to himself he ought to bear, for teaching is commended by longsuffering; but where the salvation of others is at stake, forbearance is not meekness but coldness, and he must interpose with authority.

debates.question: Is 'let no man despise thy youth' a charge to give no occasion, or to assert authority?

sides.position: Give no occasion: act so that nobody shall have grounds to despise you, since youth is not despised where vanities and follies are avoided
Assert the office: a priest must command authoritatively, and a man in office should not suffer himself to be treated with contempt

debates.question: How old was Timothy?

sides.position: About three and twenty, though possibly older, since Saul was called a young man at thirty or more
Not more than forty — to Paul the aged his son in the faith still seemed youthful

debates.question: What does 'in word' cover?

sides.position: Not the public teaching but the usual and familiar conversation
Both public utterance and social intercourse
Doctrine — teach nothing but the truth of God, because nothing else will save souls

outliers.note: Alone infers from this warning, taken with the note about Timothy's stomach and the request at Corinth that no man despise him, that there was nothing winning in Timothy's personal appearance — and generalises it, that beauty was the exception among the early leaders, Paul being mean and insignificant in Luther's phrase and Tertullian, Clement and Justin all describing Christ as having no human beauty, with Origen alone dissenting, because this religion was meant to owe nothing to the ordinary conditions of human success.

Alone resolves the tension between authority and meekness by separating the personal from the public: insult to himself a teacher must bear, since teaching is commended by longsuffering, but where others' salvation is concerned the same forbearance is not meekness but coldness.

Alone reads the word for purity as a standing refutation of clerical celibacy, declaring that if the apostle had wished to produce the highest possible corruption in the church he would have enjoined celibacy on the clergy and filled it with monks and nuns.

Alone treats 'in spirit' as a textual problem in detail, listing the manuscripts and versions from which it is missing and noting that Griesbach removes it from the text as probably added by a later hand — a judgement Ellicott shares but Wesley and Barnes pass over, glossing the words as though they stood.

themes: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

13.pericope_label: Give attendance to reading; neglect not the gift that is in thee

schools.summary: Correct the opening phrase: the Greek is a present indicative, so the sense is while I am coming, not till I come. Take the reading primarily as the public reading of Scripture in the congregation, a practice carried over from the synagogue, without excluding private study — and it is worth asking whether anything besides the Old Testament was read in those assemblies, since one of the older Gospels was probably already in use and Justin shows how soon that became regular. Note the order of the two words that follow and do not preach it as a sequence: exhortation needs teaching to rest upon. On the gift, trace the word through its New Testament uses and resist the idea that ordination infused a new grace; and observe that the preposition before the laying on of hands marks accompaniment, not instrument.

Supply the history the clause assumes: Paul hoped to be at Ephesus shortly and was prevented, and afterwards sent for its elders to meet him at Miletus, so the charge is not limited to the interval. On the gift, define it by exclusion. It is not natural ability or capacity; it is not acquired learning, or the knowledge of languages and sciences; it is not even special saving grace, since a man may have all these and still not be apt to teach. It is a peculiar and distinct gift of interpreting the Scriptures and dispensing the mysteries of grace to the edification of others — a treasure put into an earthen vessel, which is by no means to be hid in the earth or wrapped in a napkin.

Take the reading both ways, publicly and privately, and say why it matters — expect no end without the means. Then be honest about what a minister of a later century must read: in the apostles' day the business was to state the great facts and prove them, whereas now the truth must be defended and obsolete usages explained from ancient writers, which requires Hebrew and Greek first, Latin next, and Syriac and Arabic to great advantage. Withdraw the pressure before it becomes a law: none of this is absolutely necessary, and there are many eminent ministers without such advantages. On the gift, hold that the graces of the Spirit were really received at the imposition of hands and warn that unimproved they will be withdrawn by the Head of the church.

debates.question: Is the reading public or private?

sides.position: Public reading of Scripture in the congregation, borrowed from the synagogue service
Chiefly private — a careful perusal of whatever would qualify him for the public work
Both, since reading at home is what makes a man fit to read and expound in the assembly

debates.question: Did the laying on of hands convey the gift?

sides.position: Yes: the gifts and graces of the Spirit were received at the imposition of hands, and unimproved will be withdrawn
No: no mysterious influence was conveyed by the act and no new grace infused; the gift is the whole train of circumstances by which he came to be qualified and recognised
The preposition marks accompaniment rather than instrument, so the hands attended the gift without conferring it

debates.question: What is meant by the presbytery, and what does it prove?

sides.position: A body of Christian elders acting together — decisive proof that ordination in the New Testament was never performed by one man alone
Paul's own act, with the elders joining in the solemnity
The brotherhood of presbyters at the place of ordination, probably Lystra, though an old tradition names Ephesus

debates.question: What is 'by prophecy'?

sides.position: An inspired prophet at the ordination declaring the divine intention to confer the grace
The prophetic declarations and the hopes of pious friends who had observed his fitness
Accompanied by prophecy, not bestowed by it

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into an argument for a polity, observing that a Presbyterian would describe an ordination in exactly these words and an Episcopalian would not, and that the passage can be used as it stands by the one and not by the other — then referring the reader to his own book on the government of the apostolic church.

Alone draws up a working reading list for a minister of his own century, ranking Hebrew and Greek first and Latin next, worth learning if only for Jerome, whose commentary on the whole of Scripture he judges in many respects erroneous and superficial.

Alone asks whether anything besides the Old Testament was read in the Christian assemblies of about the year 66, answers that one of the older Gospels was probably already in use, and cites Justin's description of Christian worship to show how soon that became regular.

Alone questions the order of exhortation and teaching, holding that in actual public work the reverse is meant, since exhortation needs teaching to rest upon — which he offers explicitly as a hint for preachers of his own day.

themes: Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

15.pericope_label: Meditate on these things; take heed to thyself and to the doctrine

schools.summary: Render the first verb be diligent in these things rather than meditate: it means keep on practising, and the contemplative rendering weakens the charge. The next phrase is idiomatic — be in these things — and the Latin and Greek parallels are exact, one being said of Caesar; it amounts to being up to one's ears in the work. The word for profiting means cutting a way forward, so preach it as progress that must be visible: real advance will be seen by the hearers, and the want of it understood just as well. In the last verse keep the two halves in their proper relation — without true teaching a pure life will not win souls, and the most efficient instruction is worthless if the life does not correspond. Give the saving its full weight: it looks to the day of judgement, and no lesser meaning will do.

Take the meditation as the reading pressed home: the Scriptures are to be read with care and laboriously searched, as men dig in mines for silver or golden ore, with passage compared to passage and the obscure read by the plain. Then apply the taking heed by parts, as a minister and not merely as a man — to his life, that it be exemplary; to his gifts, that they be used and not neglected; to the errors abroad, that he be not infected by them; and to his flock, which is the other part of himself. Of the doctrine require four things: that it be according to the Scriptures, that it tend to edification, that it be pure and all of a piece, and that it be delivered with boldness and plainness and defended against opposition.

Refuse the merely philological rendering of the first verb: Scripture makes no distinction between meditating and contemplating whatever others do, and true meditation is faith, hope, love and joy melted down together by the fire of the Spirit and offered up in secret. On giving oneself wholly, use Bengel's sharp form — he who is wholly in these will be little in worldly company, in other studies, in collecting books, coins or butterflies, wherein many pastors drone away a considerable part of their lives. Warn what follows neglect: the divine influence recedes, and like Samson shorn the man becomes as any other, unable to make others feel what he no longer feels. And having applied the chapter to the corruptions of one church throughout, be honest at the end about how far that application can be pressed.

debates.question: Does the first verb mean to meditate, or to be diligent in practice?

sides.position: Be diligent, keep on practising — the contemplative rendering is inaccurate
Meditate, in the full devotional sense: faith, hope, love and joy melted down together by the fire of the Spirit and offered up in secret
Both, the reading of Scripture being pressed home by laborious searching and comparison

debates.question: How is a minister said to save himself and his hearers?

sides.position: Not meritoriously: faithful labour is evidence of piety and is accepted as such, but an unfaithful minister cannot be saved
In the great day of judgement, and only the highest meaning will do — eternal happiness for pastor and flock is the double reward

outliers.note: Alone extends taking heed to thyself to manners and person, holding that there is no religion in a filthy person, in uncouth manners, in bad grammar or slovenly habits, and that to be a real gentleman should be as much a matter of conscience with a minister as to be a real Christian — religion refines the manners and never produces boorish ones.

Alone declines the identification the rest of the chapter has been building toward. Having reserved and then reproduced Bishop Newton's entire dissertation on the prophecy, he refuses to adjudicate: which mode of interpretation is best he will not attempt to say, and whether God had that church alone in view he dare not affirm.

Alone marks the ditch on both sides of the charge to take heed to oneself, noting that some young preachers are careless about their health and habits and some are too finical, and alone says plainly that it is inspiring to watch a young preacher grow because the church grows with him.

themes: Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
